routes.description: Establish Christian belief as an intellectually defensible interpretation of shared evidence and as a morally constructive framework whose governing norms, explanatory resources, and characteristic effects cannot be reduced to pathological or extremist uses.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if religious interpretation remains epistemically permissible alongside science, offers a defensible basis for meaning and morality, and supplies internal norms and practices that distinguish constructive Christianity from coercive misuse.

motionBridge.description: Connect the defensibility of religious interpretation and the constructive operation of Christian moral norms to the motion's combined intellectual and moral standard.

centralBridges.description: Show that science does not exhaust questions of existence, meaning, and value, leaving Christian belief available as a contestable interpretation of public evidence.
Explain why transcendent grounding can support moral obligation and why secular alternatives face their own justificatory burdens.
Distinguish Christianity's governing norms from extremist capture and demonstrate how those norms can criticize violence, restrain dehumanization, and motivate forgiveness.
Provide principled interpretations of sacrifice and difficult scripture that preserve restoration and moral transformation without making coercion or violence normative.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Situate historical harms alongside evidence of well-being, generosity, and constructive conduct without treating beneficial effects as proof of theological truth.
Show that psychological desire neither establishes nor refutes belief and may shape religious and atheistic commitments alike.

routes.description: Establish that religious belief exceeds the available evidence and that claims of divine authority introduce coercive doctrines, permissions, and incentives that are unnecessary for morality and capable of worsening human harm.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalistic accounts better fit the public evidence, secular human capacities adequately ground moral life, and authoritative religious doctrines add distinctive mechanisms of coercion or harm without indispensable moral benefits.

motionBridge.description: Connect evidential insufficiency and the harmful consequences of asserted divine authority to the motion's indictment of religion as unsupported and coercive.

centralBridges.description: Use cosmology, evolution, natural history, and explanatory parsimony to challenge anthropocentric design, intervention, revelation, and confident knowledge of divine commands.
Ground moral obligation in solidarity, reciprocity, and evolved social capacities while denying that religion supplies an indispensable or uniquely moral act.
Show how canonical texts, doctrines, and claimed divine commands can authorize conduct ordinarily judged cruel, coercive, or lethal.
Explain how surveillance, compulsory obedience, threatened punishment, salvation conditions, and eschatological authority make religious commitment coercive rather than freely optional.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Separate religious welfare or consolation effects from the truth of theological claims and from conclusions about religion's general moral character.
Answer secular atrocity comparisons by examining religious alliances and the transfer of faith, messianism, and unquestioned obedience into political movements.

sections.title: Public Evidence, Science, and Religious Explanation
sections.rationale: This issue tests the intellectual half of the motion by comparing naturalistic accounts of cosmology and human history with the claim that science leaves legitimate room for transcendent meaning and Christian interpretation.

sections.title: Divine and Secular Grounds of Moral Obligation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether transcendent foundations are needed to justify moral judgments or whether solidarity, reciprocity, and evolved social capacities can sustain obligation without divine authority.

sections.title: Religious Harm, Extremism, and Constructive Effects
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether violence and social harm are characteristic consequences of religion or products of broader human and ideological extremism, while also testing the relevance and limits of claimed constructive effects.

sections.title: Scripture, Salvation, Sacrifice, and Coercive Authority
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether foundational texts and doctrines normalize sacrifice, punishment, and compelled obedience or admit principled interpretations centered on voluntary restoration and nonviolent moral correction.

sections.title: Consolation, Human Dignity, and Worldview Motivation
sections.rationale: This issue tests psychological explanations of belief and unbelief, including whether religion rests on consoling desire, degrades or elevates human dignity, or offers meaning without converting desire into evidence.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-06.proposition: McGrath's movement from scientific atheism to Christianity arose from intellectual scrutiny and perceived explanatory coherence rather than wish fulfillment or psychological need.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-10.proposition: The nonviolent example of Jesus supplies Christianity with an internal norm for criticizing violent adherents and can inspire forgiveness rather than retaliation.

chunk-002:c002-01.proposition: Science cannot by its legitimate methods adjudicate God's existence, and nature remains open to atheist, agnostic, or Christian interpretation rather than forcing atheism.

chunk-002:c002-02.proposition: Secular moral systems face a justificatory problem because evolved tendencies, postmodern critique, and cultural manipulation do not by themselves secure moral obligation against interested power.

chunk-002:c002-08.proposition: A desire for God neither establishes nor disproves God's reality, and atheism may likewise satisfy a psychological desire for liberation from divine accountability.

chunk-003:c003-01.proposition: Christ's death can be understood through several transformative biblical models as a freely offered possibility of purification and restoration rather than an imposed transaction.

chunk-003:c003-05.proposition: Science explains relationships within material order but does not exhaust questions of meaning and value, leaving transcendent religious interpretation as a legitimate complementary perspective.

chunk-003:c003-06.proposition: Christ and progressive revelation provide Christians with a principled basis for challenging violent surface readings of Old Testament passages rather than treating them as timeless commands.

chunk-003:c003-08.proposition: Loving enemies does not require moral indifference; it can restrain violence by preserving opponents' humanity while permitting clear opposition to wrongdoing.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-01.proposition: Christian vicarious redemption is morally objectionable because punishing one person cannot erase another individual's responsibility for wrongdoing.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-02.proposition: Monotheism is structurally coercive because it subjects people without consent to divine surveillance, compulsory obedience, punishment, and judgment even for their thoughts.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-03.proposition: Accepting religious consolation at the expense of truthfulness, or claiming that moral discrimination comes only from divine command, compromises human intellectual integrity and innate moral agency.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-04.proposition: Christian revelation is difficult to reconcile with humanity's long natural history because a late and localized divine intervention implies a designer who tolerated immense suffering through ineptitude, cruelty, or indifference.

chunk-001:chunk-001-candidate-05.proposition: Religion combines the abasement of human beings as sinful and shameful with the anthropocentric flattery that the universe was designed especially for them.

chunk-002:c002-03.proposition: Health, well-being, or welfare benefits associated with religious belief establish neither the truth of its theological claims nor the benign character of religion generally.

chunk-002:c002-06.proposition: Believers cannot identify a uniquely religious moral act unavailable to unbelievers, while supposed divine commands can provide distinctively religious motives for wicked conduct.

chunk-002:c002-07.proposition: Twentieth-century totalitarian atrocities do not vindicate religion when fascist movements allied with churches and other regimes reproduced religious habits of credulity, obedience, faith, and messianism.

chunk-003:c003-04.proposition: Human solidarity, reciprocity, mutual aid, and evolved social capacities can sustain moral obligation without divine permission, while naturalistic explanation avoids unnecessary supernatural assumptions.

chunk-003:c003-09.proposition: Cosmic scale, extinction, and evolution make anthropocentric design improbable, and even allowing an unknown originating mind would not justify confident claims about revelation, miracles, or specific divine commands.
